c.tagline: Okanagan wine country on a sun-soaked lake, ringed by vineyards, beaches, and ski slopes.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares start around C$3.50 plus per-km charges. Kelowna Cabs and the local Current Taxi app operate citywide; Uber and Lyft also serve Kelowna and are often cheaper.

emergency.note: 911 is the single emergency number for police, fire, and ambulance across Canada; 811 (HealthLink BC) is the non-emergency health advice line.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Some street disorder around the Leon Avenue area downtown late at night.

hood_desc: The walkable core along Bernard Avenue and the Okanagan Lake waterfront, packed with restaurants, breweries, City Park beach, the marina, and the Kelowna Art Gallery; the best base for first-time visitors who want to be in the middle of everything.

A relaxed lakeside village just south of downtown with cafes, boutiques, the Pandosy Waterfront Park, and Gyro Beach; suits travelers who want beach access and a local, low-key vibe within reach of the centre.
A leafy, upscale residential area stretching along the lake south of Pandosy, home to sandy beaches, parks, and easy access to Mission-area wineries; good for families and a quiet, resort-style stay.
Kelowna's craft-brewery and light-industrial district north of downtown below Knox Mountain, with tasting rooms, indie eateries, and hiking trails; suits younger travelers and beer-and-outdoors fans.

A more affordable, diverse residential hub east of the centre with big-box shopping, international restaurants, and quick highway access to the airport and Big White ski resort; good for budget-conscious travelers with a car.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink throughout the city.

transit.hours: Buses run roughly 6:00am to 11:00pm on most routes, with reduced service on evenings, weekends, and holidays; there is no rapid transit, so ride-hail or a car fills late-night gaps.
transit.note: Kelowna has no rail, metro, or tram; the BC Transit bus network (including frequent routes along Highway 97 and to UBC Okanagan) is the only public transit, and a car is the easiest way to reach lakeside wineries, beaches, and Big White ski resort.
transit.pay: Pay cash on board (exact fare, about C$2.50) or tap the reloadable Umo card or Umo mobile app that BC Transit uses in Kelowna. A DayPASS is about C$5, and single-ride transfers are valid for connecting buses.

bus: BC Transit Kelowna Regional Transit System
Ebus / FlixBus (intercity to Vancouver, Kamloops, Vernon)

landmarks: Okanagan Lake and City Park
Kelowna's sparkling 135-kilometre lake meets downtown at sandy Hot Sands Beach, where the iconic white Sails sculpture marks the city's favourite gathering place.
Myra Canyon Trestles
Cycle across eighteen restored wooden railway trestles and through two tunnels on the Kettle Valley Rail Trail, suspended high above a spectacular canyon.
Knox Mountain Park
A short hike or drive up Kelowna's beloved mountain park delivers sweeping viewpoints over Okanagan Lake, the bridge and vineyard-striped hillsides.
Mission Hill Family Estate Winery
This monastery-like hilltop winery in West Kelowna, with its 12-storey bell tower and outdoor amphitheatre, is the Okanagan wine country's grandest showpiece.
Waterfront Park and Ogopogo Statue
A lakeside boardwalk winds past marinas and lagoons to the playful statue of Ogopogo, the lake monster of Okanagan legend.
Father Pandosy Mission
The Okanagan Valley's first European settlement, this 1859 Oblate mission preserves original squared-log buildings that seeded Kelowna's founding.
Kasugai Gardens
A tranquil walled Japanese garden downtown, gifted through Kelowna's sister-city bond with Kasugai, with koi ponds, lanterns and meticulously pruned pines.
Summerhill Pyramid Winery
Canada's most-visited organic winery ages its sparkling wine inside a precise replica pyramid, pairing eccentric charm with sweeping vineyard-and-lake views.
Okanagan Heritage Museum
Downtown's engaging museum traces the valley's story from syilx First Nations culture through fur trading and the orchard boom that built Kelowna.
Big White Ski Resort
An hour's drive east, this champagne-powder resort famous for its snow ghosts offers the Okanagan's premier skiing and summer alpine day trips.

train.note: Kelowna has no passenger railway - the Okanagan lines closed to passengers decades ago and the Kettle Valley trackbed is now a rail trail. The nearest VIA Rail service is at Kamloops, about two hours north. Travel by coach or fly into Kelowna's airport, which has good domestic connections.

bus.note: No international coaches. Ebus (https://myebus.ca/) runs from Kelowna to Vancouver in about 6 hours, Kamloops and Vernon, with Rider Express (https://riderexpress.ca/) on some routes east toward Calgary. Since Greyhound Canada left western Canada, the interior is thinly served - book ahead and check which days services run.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled ferry on Okanagan Lake - the old Kelowna ferry was replaced by the William R. Bennett floating bridge. Lake cruises and boat rentals are recreational. BC's inland free car ferries operate elsewhere in the Kootenays.
